line: Jung on ten in the traditional symbolism (CW10 ¶692) and on the tetraktys, and von Franz on ten in Number and Time.

sections.title: The completed cycle
sections.line: CW10 ¶692 (Flying Saucers, 1958): in the interpretation of a dream of the numbers eight and eleven, ten as the perfect unfolding of unity and the numbers one to ten as a completed cycle.

quotes.quote: Ten is the perfect unfolding of unity, and the numbers one to ten have the significance of a completed cycle
10 + 1 = 11 therefore denotes the beginning of a new cycle

sections.title: The tetraktys
sections.line: CW11 ¶246 (the Trinity essay): the Pythagorean oath and the tetraktys; CW10 ¶805: the number 4, the Pythagorean tetraktys; Number and Time: von Franz on the tetractys as the sum of 1, 2, 3 and 4.

quotes.quote: the Pythagorean oath, for instance, says that the tetraktys “contains the roots of eternal nature.”
This is true particularly of the number 4, the Pythagorean tetraktys.
The famous Pythagorean tetractys consists of the sum of 1, 2, 3, and 4 (= 10).

sections.title: Von Franz on ten
sections.line: Number and Time: von Franz on Fa-tsang's simile of ten copper coins, in which ten signifies the whole inexhaustible multiplicity of existence and the one is integrated into the ten; and on the sephiroth as the ten primal numbers.

quotes.quote: in which ten here signifies the whole inexhaustible multiplicity of existence
One contains no power (wu-l) in itself and is therefore integrated into the ten
Ten, however, represents the ten in one
the ten primal numbers, the sephiroth, are considered to be emanations of divine immaterial origin
